text: Tissue repair after injury involves overlapping events—inflammation, re-epithelialization, neovascularization, and synthesis/stabilization of a fibrous extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeled over time. Members of the transglutaminase (TG) family are upregulated during wound healing and act as a novel class of wound-healing mediators. These enzymes crosslink proteins via ε(γ-glutamyl)lysine bridges, stabilizing proteins and regulating the behavior of diverse cell types recruited to the damaged area for repair. The article examines tissue transglutaminase (TG2), the most widely expressed TG family member, in wound repair. Drawing on early and recent literature, the authors show that multifunctional TG2 affects ECM stability, cell–ECM interactions, and consequently cell behavior across the different phases of wound healing, and highlight how TG2 itself might be exploited therapeutically.
